paras: The threatened lynching of Frank Shank was a written demand, dated at East Germantown, Indiana, on May 28, 1888, that the sheriff of Wayne County surrender Shank to 'Judge Lynch' at midnight on May 29. Shank was then in jail, accused of cutting the throat of Lulu Penny, a young schoolteacher who had rejected him. No report of an attack on the jail appears in the coverage.

Penny, the daughter of a farmer, had been teaching school at East Germantown, and Shank had courted her for a long time before she discarded him. According to a Cambridge City special, on the night of May 22 she was walking home with Frank Winter when, as Winter stepped over a fence, Shank seized her, cut three gashes in her throat and walked away. A Richmond dispatch added a cut to her cheek and reported that Shank, jailed, said he was drunk and supposed he had done it while she was upbraiding him.

Reports of her condition differed: one brief gave 'small hope of recovery', the Richmond dispatch said physicians first thought the wounds fatal but were later hopeful, and the Cambridge City report said she would live. The Cambridge City report also noted 'intense excitement' in the neighborhood, and another brief described Shank as 'a notorious character' who had shot a man there the previous fall.

On May 29 Sheriff Bond found in his mail a letter addressed to the 'Sheriff of Wayne County' and signed 'COMMITTEE'. It ordered him to deliver Shank to 'Judge Lynch' at midnight that night 'to 100 armed men, masked at the door', warned 'Tell no one to deny in danger of life', and asserted that 'The girl is going to die.'
The coverage does not show whether anyone came to the jail on the night of May 29, how the sheriff responded, or what became of Shank's case or Penny's recovery.

Only the Indianapolis Journal reported the threat, printing the letter in full in a Richmond dispatch headed 'A Summons from Judge Lynch' without comment. The dispatch itself took a harsh view of the prisoner, calling him 'the worthless fellow who so murderously assaulted' Penny, a phrase that echoed the Richmond special's 'a worthless fellow'.

Papers outside Indiana carried only the assault, as a one-line 'Pointed Paragraphs' item in the Maysville Evening Bulletin and the Huntsville Gazette, a brief in the Mitchell Capital in Dakota, and a longer special under 'A Lover's Crime' in the Louisville Weekly Courier-Journal. None of these reports mentioned a lynching threat or the race of anyone involved.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Frank Shank
bases: A letter signed 'Committee' demanded that the Wayne County sheriff hand the jailed Frank Shank to 'Judge Lynch' and 100 armed, masked men; no attack is reported (A7).

No one was killed: the only report is of a threatening letter demanding Shank's delivery to 'Judge Lynch' (A7); the claimed 100 masked men are the letter's own words, and no report shows any group assembling.
The threat letter appears only in the Indianapolis Journal's Richmond dispatch (A7); the assault that prompted it is reported independently by several papers (A1, A4, A6).

versions.value: Injuries pronounced fatal, then physicians sanguine of recovery
'The girl is going to die' (the Committee's claim)

conflicts.note: The physicians' later view (A4) and the local Cambridge City special (A6) are better evidence on her condition than the threat letter, which states the writers' claim.

record_check.dossier: Letter dated May 28 and found by the sheriff May 29; May 29 at midnight was the demanded deadline. The assault behind it was on the night of May 22.
Supported: Shank was in jail and the letter demanded the sheriff deliver him.
The threat appears in one paper; the underlying assault ran in at least five other white papers May 25-30.
